name: Famulor
tagline: AI voice agents that answer and place phone calls, book appointments, and push the results into your CRM.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The pieces of a phone agent are all rentable now: Twilio gives you a number and a media stream, Deepgram does streaming speech to text, any decent LLM does the reasoning, ElevenLabs does the voice. An agent can wire that into a working single-line receptionist that answers, talks, and logs a transcript in a weekend, and it will feel uncannily close on your first test call. What does not come free is the boring 20 percent: barge-in that does not talk over the caller, latency under a second on a bad mobile connection, warm transfer to a human, retry logic on outbound campaigns, and a calendar booking flow that does not hallucinate a slot. Famulor is also selling a no-code agent builder plus CRM and calendar wiring plus EU telephony and recording-consent hygiene, none of which your build has. If you need one AI answering one line for yourself, build it; if you need a fleet of them talking to paying customers, do not.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted phone number that answers inbound calls with a streaming speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech loop, follows a prompt-defined script, and writes a transcript plus structured outcome to a local database.
requirements: A Twilio account and a purchased phone number
API keys for a streaming STT provider, an LLM, and a TTS provider
A publicly reachable HTTPS/WSS endpoint, so a small VPS or a tunnel
Per-minute telephony and model spend, which you pay either way
Tolerance for tuning turn detection until it stops interrupting people
whatYouLose: No-code agent builder and prompt versioning, so every script change is a code or config edit
Prebuilt CRM, calendar, and webhook integrations for booking and lead handoff
Outbound campaign machinery: lists, pacing, retries, voicemail detection, do-not-call handling
Someone else owning call quality, codec issues, and carrier weirdness at 3am
Recording consent flows, data residency, and the audit trail you want if these calls touch real customers
moatNotes: The model layer is commodity. The defensible parts are the CRM/calendar connectors, the latency and interruption tuning, and being the party that signed the data processing agreement.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a demo call and a production phone line are different products. Businesses buying this are not buying speech recognition, they are buying the fact that when a customer calls at 7pm the agent answers in 700ms, does not talk over them, books the right slot in the real calendar, and leaves a record someone can audit. Getting from a working weekend prototype to that is weeks of unglamorous tuning plus ongoing carrier babysitting, and most buyers would rather expense a subscription than own a telephony stack.
notes: Great weekend project, mediocre business replacement: the fun part is one evening, the reliability is the whole rest of the year.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted AI phone agent that answers inbound calls on a single phone number. Empty folder, start from scratch.

Stack, no substitutions:
- TypeScript on Node 20, Fastify for HTTP, the ws package for WebSockets
- Twilio Voice with Media Streams for telephony (bidirectional audio over WSS)
- Deepgram streaming STT for transcription
- OpenAI chat completions with streaming for the agent brain
- ElevenLabs streaming TTS for the voice, mu-law 8kHz output to match Twilio
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for call records
- No React, no auth, no cloud dashboard, no telemetry

What to build:
1. POST /voice returns TwiML that opens a bidirectional Media Stream to /media.
2. /media WebSocket handler: decode inbound mu-law frames, pipe to Deepgram streaming with interim results and endpointing, and on each finalized utterance call the LLM with the running conversation plus a system prompt loaded from agent.md.
3. Stream the LLM response sentence by sentence into ElevenLabs, encode to mu-law 8kHz, and send back as Twilio media frames. Implement barge-in: if new caller speech is detected while the agent is speaking, clear the Twilio audio queue and stop the current TTS stream.
4. Give the agent exactly two tools: get_availability and book_slot, backed by a local slots table in SQLite. No external calendar.
5. Persist every call: caller number, start and end time, full transcript with speaker labels, tool calls made, and a one-line LLM-generated summary written after hangup.
6. A single server-rendered page at / listing calls newest first, with a detail view showing the transcript. Plain HTML, no client framework.
7. Log per-turn latency (speech end to first audio byte out) to stdout so tuning is possible.

Out of scope, do not build: outbound calling, campaigns, multi-agent management, a visual flow builder, human transfer, CRM connectors, multi-tenancy, billing, call recording audio storage.

All credentials in .env: TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, DEEPGRAM_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, ELEVENLABS_API_KEY, ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID. Ship a .env.example and a README with the exact Twilio console steps to point a number at /voice, plus a note that a public HTTPS tunnel is required for local testing. Include one script that replays a recorded wav file through the pipeline so the loop can be tested without burning call minutes.
